data.title: Hailey–Hailey disease — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hailey–Hailey disease** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Write short notes on Hailey–Hailey disease (PYQ).**
- Familial benign chronic pemphigus — autosomal dominant ATP2C1 mutation (SPCA1 — Golgi Ca²⁺/Mn²⁺ ATPase) → defective desmosome assembly → suprabasal acantholysis; onset in 3rd–4th decade

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Recurrent flaccid vesicles and erosions on erythematous base in intertriginous areas (neck, axillae, groin, perianal, submammary), with crusting, painful fissures ('cracked/ dried mud' or 'rhagades'), maceration and foul odour; worse with heat, sweat, friction, infection
- Nails: longitudinal white bands (asymptomatic); mucosa rarely involved
- Segmental/linear types (mosaic)

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Suprabasal and full-thickness acantholysis with partially attached keratinocytes giving a 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance, few dyskeratotic cells (fewer than Darier's), DIF negative

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Intertrigo (candidal, bacterial, tinea — KOH/culture), pemphigus vegetans (DIF positive), Darier's disease, inverse psoriasis, erythrasma, contact dermatitis, impetigo, HSV

**Q5. Management.**
- Avoid friction/heat/sweating, weight loss, loose clothing; treat secondary infections (antibiotics, antifungals, antivirals)
- Topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, antiseptics, calcitriol
- Oral: doxycycline/minocycline (anti-inflammatory), dapsone, acitretin, low-dose naltrexone (newer evidence), cyclosporine short-term, oral magnesium, glycopyrrolate (sweat)
- Botulinum toxin to reduce sweating in flexures
- Procedures: CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, dermabrasion, PDT, excision with grafting for refractory localised disease

**Q6. Differentiate Darier's and Hailey–Hailey diseases.**
- Darier's: ATP2A2 (SERCA2, ER), seborrhoeic areas + flexures, keratotic papules, nail red-white bands with V-notch, palmar pits, oral papules, neuropsychiatric associations; histology — prominent dyskeratosis (corps ronds, grains)
- Hailey–Hailey: ATP2C1 (SPCA1, Golgi), flexures only, vesicles/erosions/fissures, nails white bands only, no mucosa; histology — dilapidated brick wall, little dyskeratosis

**Q7. Clinical features in detail.**
- Familial benign chronic pemphigus: onset 3rd–4th decade; recurrent flaccid vesicles and erosions in flexures (neck sides, axillae, groin, perianal, submammary) forming macerated, fissured plaques ('cerebriform' rhagades), malodour, pain; longitudinal white lines on fingernails; worse with heat, sweat, friction, infection

**Q8. Histopathology in detail.**
- Widespread suprabasal and intraepidermal acantholysis with partially attached cells — 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance; few dyskeratotic cells (fewer than Darier); DIF negative (vs pemphigus)

**Q9. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Pemphigus vegetans (DIF positive), intertrigo (candidal, bacterial), inverse psoriasis, flexural Darier's, erythrasma, tinea cruris, seborrhoeic dermatitis, extramammary Paget's, contact dermatitis

**Q10. Laser and procedural treatments.**
- CO2 or Er:YAG ablation of affected skin (re-epithelialisation from adnexa with normal cells reduces recurrences), dermabrasion, PDT, excision with grafting; botulinum toxin in axillae/ groin; long remissions reported

**Q11. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- Chronic relapsing course with flares in summer; does not affect life expectancy; may improve with age

**Q13. What is the genetic basis?**
- Autosomal dominant ATP2C1 mutation → defective SPCA1 (Golgi calcium/manganese pump) → impaired desmosome assembly → suprabasal acantholysis ('dilapidated brick wall' appearance)

**Q14. What newer treatments help?**
- Botulinum toxin A (reduces sweating — fewer flares), low-dose naltrexone (1.5–4.5 mg/day — reported benefit), dupilumab/apremilast (case reports), oral magnesium chloride, glycopyrrolate, laser ablation (CO2, Er:YAG), PDT, dermabrasion; topical steroids/ tacrolimus/ antibiotics/ antifungals for flares

**Q15. Why is secondary infection a problem?**
- Macerated flexural erosions get colonised by S. aureus, Candida and HSV — flares; swab and treat; consider HSV if sudden painful worsening (Kaposi's varicelliform eruption)

## Quick spotter facts
- Recurrent flexural erosions with fissures in adults with family history — Hailey–Hailey (ATP2C1)
- Dilapidated brick wall

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hailey–Hailey disease). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
